warmup.q: In a flame graph of the report step, the box for String.format sits to the left of Pattern.compile, at the same height. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing about time: boxes at the same level are sorted alphabetically by frame name
warmup.why: Left to right in a flame graph isn't a timeline. flamegraph.pl says the ordering "has no meaning" and sorts frames alphabetically: java/lang/String.format comes before java/util/regex/Pattern.compile. Width says how many samples had the frame; height says how deep the stack was. A caller is drawn below its callees, never beside them.

opening:
Picture the restaurant's manager, who wants to know where the evening goes without asking anyone to fill in a timesheet. Every few seconds she glances through the kitchen door and notes what each cook is doing, and for which dish: "Ana, soup, chopping onions." After a night of glances, the tally tells the story. If a third of her notes say "chopping onions", about a third of the evening went on onions.

A sampling profiler does that to your program. In lesson 5, JFR's sampler gave us only 40 glances in 4 seconds; this lesson takes thousands.

There's a trap. A manager who only glances when a cook puts the knife down sees many cooks at the sink and few at the cutting board. The hand-made profiler we'll build has the same habit: it blamed up to 29% of the time on a method whose real work happens in the methods it calls. In this lesson, we'll build that sampler, catch it out, profile the same code with async-profiler, read the answer as a flame graph and pick the right kind of sample for each question. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a manager who glances into the kitchen every few seconds, and a second one who only looks up when a cook puts the knife down. Our hand-made sampler was the second: it blamed String.split for work its inlined callees did. async-profiler looks at any moment, and a flame graph turns its tally into boxes whose width is time.

Now take a profile of a program of yours and find the widest bare top. Follow it down to the first frame in your own code: that's the line to read.

Next, we'll put every tool so far into one investigation. Starting from "it's slow", how do we reach a fix we can prove to the byte?

sections.h: A sampling profiler is a loop that counts stacks
sections.html:
Here's the code we'll profile in this lesson and the next. It's the report service's busiest step. It checks a document's language, counts its words and works out the reading time. Then it writes a line for the debug log, a level of logging that's usually switched off. The result is right, and the code looks harmless:

Java
static long readingSeconds(Document d) {
    if (!Pattern.compile("^[a-z]{2}$").matcher(d.language()).matches())   // a regex compiled per call
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language");
    long words = d.text().split(" ").length;                               // a new String for every word
    long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238;                               // 238 words a minute, rounded up
    debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d",     // formatted, then thrown away
            d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds));
    return seconds;
}
Kotlin
fun kReadingSeconds(d: KDocument): Long {
    require(Regex("^[a-z]{2}$").matches(d.language)) { "bad language" }   // a regex compiled per call
    val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong()                          // a new String for every word
    val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238                               // 238 words a minute, rounded up
    kDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d"                 // formatted, then thrown away
        .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds))
    return seconds
}

We want to know where its CPU time goes, call by call, without changing it. We could put timers around every line, but timers change what they measure, and we'd need to know where to put them first.

A sampling profiler does something simpler. Every few milliseconds it looks at what each thread is running, writes down the thread's whole call stack, and counts how often each stack turns up. A thread is one line of work inside a program. Its call stack is the chain of methods it's inside right now, from Thread.run at the bottom to the running method at the top. If a method is on top in 20% of the samples, the thread spent about 20% of its time there. That's the manager's tally: one glance is a sample, and "Ana, soup, chopping onions" is a stack, read from the bottom up.

You can build one in a dozen lines:

Java
Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>();
while (worker.isAlive()) {
    Thread.sleep(10);                                       // 1. wait one sampling interval
    StackTraceElement[] st = worker.getStackTrace();        // 2. snapshot the thread's stack
    List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)                // 3. root first
        frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName());
    stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum);  // 4. count identical stacks
}
Kotlin
val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>()
while (worker.isAlive) {
    Thread.sleep(10)                                        // 1. wait one sampling interval
    val st = worker.stackTrace                              // 2. snapshot the thread's stack
    val key = st.reversed()                                 // 3. root first
        .joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" }
    stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus)                       // 4. count identical stacks
}

The output is called collapsed stacks, the text format that flame-graph tools read. Each distinct stack gets one line: its frames from the root to the top, separated by ;, then the number of samples. A frame is one method call on the stack. Here's a real line:

java.lang.Thread.run;workbench.performance.l06.SlowReport.lambda$hammer$0;workbench.performance.l06.SlowReport.readingSeconds;java.lang.String.split;java.lang.String.split;java.lang.String.split 60

Two words come up all the time. A frame's self time is the samples where it was on top of the stack, doing the work itself. Its inclusive time adds everything it called. readingSeconds has little self time and a large inclusive time: it does little on its own and calls expensive things.

PoorMansProfiler runs the step on two threads for 4 seconds and samples them this way. One run on the busy course machine took 238 samples. That's fewer than the 800 the arithmetic promises, because the sampler's own thread didn't always get a CPU core on time. Its top frames:

238 samples; top frames:
   29.4%  java.lang.String.split
   13.4%  java.util.Formatter.format
   12.6%  java.util.Formatter.parse
    7.1%  java.util.regex.Pattern.sequence
    5.9%  java.util.regex.Pattern.clazz
    5.9%  java.util.regex.Pattern.compile

That looks like a usable answer: splitting the text is the biggest cost. Is it really? The next section says no.

try.title: Run a profiler you can read in one screen
steps: Read PoorMansProfiler and SlowReport.readingSeconds. Predict the three methods that will be on top most often.
Run it. It prints the top frames and writes build/poor-man.collapsed (inside labs/performance).
Open the collapsed file and find the line with the biggest count. How many frames deep is it, and what's on top? Then run the Kotlin twin and compare its top frames.

code.title: PoorMansProfiler.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * A sampling profiler in 40 lines: every 10 ms, take the stack of each worker thread with * Thread.getStackTrace() and count it. Writes the samples as collapsed stacks, the text format * flame graph tools read, to build/poor-man.collapsed. */ public class PoorMansProfiler { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long until = System.nanoTime() + 4_000_000_000L; Thread work = new Thread(() -> { try { SlowReport.hammer(2, until); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); work.start(); Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); // "frame;frame;frame" -> samples while (work.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); for (Thread t : Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet()) { if (!t.getName().startsWith("report-")) continue; StackTraceElement[] st = t.getStackTrace(); // the JVM must pause t to walk its stack if (st.length == 0) continue; List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) // root first, as flame graphs want frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName()); stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum); } } write(stacks, Path.of("build", "poor-man.collapsed")); Map<String, Long> self = new HashMap<>(); // top frame = where the thread was stacks.forEach((k, v) -> self.merge(k.substring(k.lastIndexOf(';') + 1), v, Long::sum)); long total = self.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); System.out.println(total + " samples; top frames:"); self.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(6) .forEach(e -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * e.getValue() / total, e.getKey())); } static void write(Map<String, Long> stacks, Path file) throws IOException { Files.createDirectories(file.getParent()); List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>(); stacks.forEach((k, v) -> lines.add(k + " " + v)); Files.write(file, lines); System.out.println("collapsed stacks written to " + file.toAbsolutePath()); } }

alt.title: PoorMansProfiler.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l06 import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of PoorMansProfiler.java: every 10 ms, take the stack of each worker thread with // Thread.getStackTrace() and count it. Writes collapsed stacks to build/poor-man-kt.collapsed. fun main() { val until = System.nanoTime() + 4_000_000_000L val work = thread { kHammer(2, until) } val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>() // "frame;frame;frame" -> samples while (work.isAlive) { Thread.sleep(10) for (t in Thread.getAllStackTraces().keys) { if (!t.name.startsWith("report-")) continue val st = t.stackTrace // the JVM must pause t to walk its stack if (st.isEmpty()) continue val key = st.reversed().joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" } // root first stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus) } } val file = Path.of("build", "poor-man-kt.collapsed") Files.createDirectories(file.parent) Files.write(file, stacks.map { (k, v) -> "$k $v" }) println("collapsed stacks written to ${file.toAbsolutePath()}") val self = stacks.entries.groupBy({ it.key.substringAfterLast(';') }, { it.value }).mapValues { it.value.sum() } val total = self.values.sum() println("$total samples; top frames:") self.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take(6) .forEach { (frame, n) -> println(" %5.1f%% %s".format(100.0 * n / total, frame)) } }

try.expect: A few hundred samples in 4 seconds (2 threads, one sample each every 10 ms if the machine keeps up; 238 in a busy run here). The top frames are String.split (19 to 29% in two runs), then Formatter and regex methods. The biggest line ends in String.split;String.split;String.split: three split frames and nothing above them. The Kotlin twin shows kotlin.text.StringsKt__StringsKt.split$StringsKt__StringsKt on top, Kotlin's own split. Remember that nothing ever sits above split for the next section.

sections.h: Safepoint bias: the hand-made sampler only sees threads where they can stop
sections.html:
Thread.getStackTrace() on another thread can't read that thread's stack at just any instruction. Compiled code keeps values in the processor's registers, and it has small methods inlined, copied into their callers (lesson 2). So the JVM can only describe a thread's stack at a safepoint: a place in the code where it has written down the full state of every frame. Compiled code checks for a request to stop at safepoint polls, which sit mostly at method returns and at the jumps back to the top of a loop. So when the sampler asks, the thread runs on to its next poll and reports its stack from there.

That's the manager who only glances when a cook puts the knife down. Samples pile up at the polls instead of where the CPU spends its time. A tight inlined loop with no poll looks free, and the method that holds the next poll gets the blame. This is safepoint bias, and every profiler built on getStackTrace, or on the JVM's tool interface call GetAllStackTraces, has it.

Our sampler shows it. String.split came top with 29.4%, and every one of its stacks ended at split itself, three frames deep. Not one sample caught the methods that split calls to find each space and copy each word. They're inlined, and by the time the thread reached a poll, they had returned. A second run put 19.3% on split and 15.8% on Formatter.parse, the same pattern.

async-profiler is an open-source profiler for the JVM, and version 4.6 is the one used here. It samples without the bias. It interrupts each thread with a signal from the operating system, driven by Linux perf_events or by a timer. Then it walks the stack at the exact instruction where the signal landed. To make sense of compiled frames there, it reads HotSpot's internal structures, including the records of which methods were inlined where.

The same code under async-profiler 4.6 on JDK 25, four threads for 10 seconds, gave 3,569 samples. Its top self frames were readingSeconds 7.2%, String.split 5.8%, StringLatin1.indexOf 5.1% and Pattern.compile 4.0%. So split itself does about a fifth of what our sampler claimed. The rest is spread over indexOf (searching for the next space), ArrayList.add and StringLatin1.newString (building each word), exactly the frames the hand-made profiler never saw. Because it works below the JVM, async-profiler also shows native code, the JVM's own threads and the operating system's kernel. In this run, the threads of the JIT, the part of the JVM that compiles busy methods, took 21.8% of all samples, and the garbage collector, which frees memory nobody uses, took 2.7%.

JFR, from lesson 5, doesn't have the bias in its old form either. On JDK 25 its sampler records where the thread was at the moment of the sample. Then it lets the thread finish the stack walk at its next safepoint (cooperative sampling, JEP 518).

A profiler that waits for safepoints reports where threads can stop, not where they spend their time. Check a surprising answer with async-profiler.

Check yourself: a method has one hot inlined loop and returns once, at the end. Which method would a getStackTrace profiler blame for the loop's time? (Whichever frame reaches the next safepoint poll, often the loop's own jump back or the caller after the return, not the instructions that burned the CPU.)

Thousands of honest samples are still just a long list of stacks. A flame graph turns them into a picture.

try.title: Profile the same code with async-profiler
steps: Download async-profiler from its GitHub releases page (Linux x64 or arm64, or macOS) and unpack it. bin/asprof is the launcher.
Run ProfileMe. It prints its process id and keeps four threads busy for 8 seconds.
In a second terminal, within those 8 seconds: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html <pid>. Open cpu.html in a browser.
Find String.split and look at what sits on top of it. Compare with PoorMansProfiler's list.

code.title: ProfileMe.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l06; /** * A target for async-profiler: four threads run SlowReport.readingSeconds for 8 seconds. * While it runs, attach from another terminal: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html <pid> */ public class ProfileMe { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int seconds = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 8; System.out.println("pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", running for " + seconds + " s"); System.out.println("attach with: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html " + ProcessHandle.current().pid()); SlowReport.hammer(4, System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L); System.out.println("done"); } }

alt.title: ProfileMe.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of ProfileMe.java (with SlowReport in Kotlin): four threads run kReadingSeconds for 8 seconds. // While it runs, attach from another terminal: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html <pid> data class KDocument(val id: String, val language: String, val text: String) @Volatile var kDebugEnabled = false // DEBUG logging is off, as it usually is fun kDebug(message: String) { if (kDebugEnabled) println(message) } fun kReadingSeconds(d: KDocument): Long { require(Regex("^[a-z]{2}$").matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } // a regex compiled per call val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong() // a new String for every word val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 // 238 words a minute, rounded up kDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d" // formatted, then thrown away .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } private val kWords = "the rain came early and the river rose over the old stone bridge before noon".split(' ') private val kLanguages = listOf("en", "fr", "de", "es", "it", "nl") fun kDocuments(n: Int) = Array(n) { i -> val text = (0 until 8 + i % 7).joinToString(" ") { w -> kWords[(i * 7 + w * 3) % kWords.size] } // 8 to 14 words KDocument("doc-$i", kLanguages[i % kLanguages.size], text) } fun kHammer(threads: Int, untilNanos: Long) { val ds = kDocuments(4_096) (0 until threads).map { seed -> thread(name = "report-$seed") { var sink = 0L var i = seed while (System.nanoTime() < untilNanos) sink += kReadingSeconds(ds[i++ and 4095]) if (sink == 42L) println() } }.forEach { it.join() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val seconds = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 8 val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() println("pid $pid, running for $seconds s") println("attach with: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html $pid") kHammer(4, System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L) println("done") }

try.expect: A flame graph with readingSeconds covering most of the width of the report- threads, and String.split, String.format and Pattern.compile as its widest children. This time split has frames above it, such as String.indexOf and StringLatin1.newString. On Linux you'll also see separate towers for the JIT compiler and GC threads. If asprof says perf_events are unavailable (common in containers), add -e ctimer, which works without them.

sections.h: Reading a flame graph: width is samples, left to right is the alphabet
sections.html:
A flame graph is the collapsed stacks drawn as boxes. In the kitchen, it's the manager's tally drawn as towers of blocks. The bottom block is the whole evening, every glance. On top of it sits a block for each dish, as wide as the number of glances that caught someone cooking it. On top of those sit the steps of each dish. Three rules make it readable.

Width is samples. A box's width is the number of samples that had that frame at that place in the stack: its inclusive time there. Identical frames at the same depth, under the same parent, merge into one box.

Left to right is not time. Boxes at the same level are sorted alphabetically by name. The header of flamegraph.pl, the original drawing script, says "The ordering on the x-axis has no meaning". async-profiler's guide says a flame graph "does not preserve information on when a particular stack trace was taken". A box on the left didn't run first. That's where the picture breaks: the manager's blocks for the evening would line up by clock time, and these never do.

Look at the tops. The part of a box with nothing on top of it is self time: the CPU was in that frame's own code. Wide tops are where to start. A wide box covered by its children is a caller, and the fix is usually in one of those children, or in the decision to call them.

The figure is drawn from the 3,569-sample profile of the last section. readingSeconds covers 2,546 samples, 71.3% of the total. Its widest children are String.split (24.2% of all samples), String.format (22.3%) and Pattern.compile (13.6%). Notice String.format on the far left. It isn't first because it ran first. It's first because java/lang/String.format sorts before java/lang/String.split, and both sort before java/util/regex.

Two smaller towers sit beside readingSeconds. One is os::javaTimeNanos: the demo's own loop calls System.nanoTime() before every call to check its deadline, and 64 samples landed in reading the clock. The measuring shows up in the measurement. The other tall towers belong to the JIT's compiler threads, busy for a fifth of the run, because 10 seconds is a short life for a JVM, as lesson 1 showed.

async-profiler's HTML colours frames by type: green for compiled Java, aqua for inlined Java, light green for interpreted Java, yellow for the JVM's own C++ code, red for native code and orange for the kernel. Clicking a box zooms in, and the search field highlights every frame that matches. Two variants are useful too. A reversed graph (--reverse) merges stacks from the top frame down, which gathers all the callers of one busy method. An icicle graph (--inverted) hangs from the top.

Width is time, left to right is the alphabet. Start at the widest top and walk down to your own code.

So the flame graph says split, format and the regex. Each of those questions came from a CPU profile. Some questions aren't about the CPU at all.

video.title: Reading a flame graph: counted stacks where width is samples, left to right is the alphabet, and the tops are where the CPU was

sections.h: Pick the mode for the question: cpu, wall, alloc or lock
sections.html:
A flame graph shows samples of something, and the mode decides what. async-profiler's main modes:

Mode A sample means Use it for
cpu (default) the thread was running on a CPU where CPU time goes
wall the thread existed, running or not where a request waits: the network, a lock, a sleep
alloc the thread allocated memory who creates the garbage
lock the thread waited to enter a lock contention

cpu mode takes its samples from Linux perf_events. Those can be blocked, for example when the file /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid holds 2 or more, or inside some containers. Then -e ctimer gives similar results from a timer, without the kernel frames.

wall mode samples every thread at the same rate, whether it runs, sleeps or waits, and the docs recommend it per thread: asprof -e wall -t -i 50ms -f wall.html <pid>. Remember the document store from lesson 5. A report that's slow because it waits for the store spends no CPU while it waits, so a cpu profile barely shows it, and wall shows exactly where it waits.

In alloc mode, "the top frame of every call trace is the class of the allocated object, and the counter is the heap pressure". It hooks into HotSpot when an object needs a fresh TLAB, the private stretch of heap each thread fills on its own, or has to be placed outside one. It doesn't disturb escape analysis, the JIT's trick of skipping objects that never leave a method: those never show up, because they were never made. An alloc profile of the report step put 34.1% of the allocated bytes under String.format, 33.3% under Pattern.compile and 28.2% under String.split. The top frames were byte[] 26.2%, java.lang.String 13.0% and boolean[] 11.0%: text being built and copied, and the regex's own tables. (Each class name ends in a short marker such as _[i], which the drawing uses to pick a colour; you can ignore it.)

lock mode puts the class of the lock on top, and the counter is the nanoseconds spent waiting to enter it: asprof -e lock -t -i 5ms -f lock.html <pid>.

You can also load the profiler when the JVM starts instead of attaching later, which helps inside a container: -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=cpu.collapsed,collapsed. -o collapsed (or collapsed in the agent's options) writes collapsed stacks instead of HTML, which is what the lab reads. --all switches on every mode at once, and the docs say it's not recommended for production.

Here's where today's tool stops. A profile shows where the time and the bytes go, during the seconds you recorded. It doesn't say which cost you can remove, whether removing it helps the slow requests, or what the next problem will be once this one is gone. Those questions need a whole investigation, and that's the next lesson.

Before opening it, predict the three widest children of readingSeconds in the allocation graph.
Start ProfileMe once more and attach with asprof -e wall -t -d 5 -f wall.html <pid>. How does it differ from cpu.html?

try.expect: In the allocation graph, String.format, Pattern.compile and String.split are the three wide children of readingSeconds, about a third each, and the top frames are classes such as byte[], java.lang.String and boolean[]. The wall graph is split by thread (-t). The four report- threads look much like the CPU profile, because they never wait, while main sits in Thread.join the whole time. In a 3-second run here, every thread got about 60 samples, one per 50 ms, the JVM's sleeping threads included: wall mode samples every thread equally, and a CPU profile would ignore main completely.

compare.title: The hand-made sampler in Java and Kotlin

java.title: PoorMansProfiler.java
java.html: Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); while (worker.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); // 1. wait one sampling interval StackTraceElement[] st = worker.getStackTrace(); // 2. snapshot the thread's stack List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) // 3. root first frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName()); stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum); // 4. count identical stacks }

kotlin.title: PoorMansProfiler.kt
kotlin.html: val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>() while (worker.isAlive) { Thread.sleep(10) // 1. wait one sampling interval val st = worker.stackTrace // 2. snapshot the thread's stack val key = st.reversed() // 3. root first .joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" } stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus) // 4. count identical stacks }

compare.note: Both versions call the same JVM method, Thread.getStackTrace(), so both share its safepoint bias and its cost: each call stops the target thread briefly. The Kotlin twin's workload uses Regex, split(' ') and the format extension, which call the same JDK classes, so its profile has the same hot spots under slightly different names. Kotlin's split is its own function, kotlin.text.StringsKt__StringsKt.split$StringsKt__StringsKt, and Regex.matches ends in java.util.regex.Pattern. Frame names follow the compiled classes: a top-level function appears under its file class, such as ProfileMeKt.kReadingSeconds.

worked.title: From a profile to the line to change

steps.say: The report service runs hot. Attach to it for 30 seconds in CPU mode, once as collapsed stacks you can search with grep, and once as HTML to look at.
steps.code: asprof -d 30 -e cpu -o collapsed -f /tmp/reports-cpu.collapsed <pid> asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/reports-cpu.html <pid>

steps.say: Find the widest self frames first: add up the counts by the last frame of each line. Here String.split, StringLatin1.indexOf and Pattern.compile lead.
steps.code: awk '{n=$NF; $NF=""; k=split($0,f,";"); s[f[k]]+=n} END {for (x in s) print s[x], x}' /tmp/reports-cpu.collapsed | sort -rn | head -5

steps.say: A JDK frame on top is rarely the thing to fix. Walk down each busy stack to the first frame in your own package. Self-check: why stop at your own frame and not at the JDK one? (You can't make String.split faster, but you can stop asking it to build a String for every word.)
steps.code:
java/lang/StringLatin1.indexOf                       <- top, JDK
java/lang/String.split                               <- JDK
workbench/performance/l06/SlowReport.readingSeconds  <- first frame you own: the line to change

steps.say: Fix one thing, profile again, and compare the widths. Lesson 7 does exactly this, and finds that the next problem only stands out once the first one is gone.

lab.title: Build a flame graph from collapsed stacks
steps: Run the tests. All five fail. The fixture is seven real lines from an async-profiler 4.6 profile of SlowReport.readingSeconds on JDK 25.
Write parse. Frame names can contain spaces (itable stub), so split on the last space.
Write selfTime (the count goes to the last frame) and inclusiveTime (the count goes to every distinct frame in the stack, once).
Write build with the FlameNode class provided: walk each stack from the root, adding the count to every node on the way. FlameNode keeps its children sorted by name, like flamegraph.pl.
Write hottestPath, then run the tests until all five pass. Optional: run your code on build/poor-man.collapsed from the first Try it.
hints: line.lastIndexOf(' ') splits the count off. split(';') gives the frames, root first.

In the fixture, String.split appears three times in one stack (the public split(String) and two private versions it calls), and Pattern.compile twice. Counting every appearance gives 237 instead of 79 for split: use frames.toSet().
In build, start with root.total += count, then node = node.child(frame); node.total += count for each frame. Equal prefixes merge by themselves, because child returns the existing node.
FlameNode.self is already there: the total minus the children's totals. You don't store it.

drill.title: Collapse and count from memory
drill.prompt:
Close this page. Given these collapsed lines, write down the self time and the inclusive time of b, and draw the flame graph as boxes with widths:

a;b;c 3
a;b 2
a;d;b 1

Then write the code that computes inclusive time from a list of samples.

answer.html: // self(b) = 2 (only "a;b" ends in b); inclusive(b) = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 // flame graph, root at the bottom, children in alphabetical order: // [c 3] [b 1] // [b 5 ][d 1 ] // [a 6 ] static Map<String, Long> inclusive(List<Sample> samples) { Map<String, Long> result = new HashMap<>(); for (Sample s : samples) { for (String frame : new HashSet<>(s.frames())) { // once per sample result.merge(frame, s.count(), Long::sum); } } return result; }

alt.html: // self(b) = 2 (only "a;b" ends in b); inclusive(b) = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 // flame graph, root at the bottom, children in alphabetical order: // [c 3] [b 1] // [b 5 ][d 1 ] // [a 6 ] fun inclusive(samples: List<Sample>): Map<String, Long> { val result = HashMap<String, Long>() for (s in samples) { for (frame in s.frames.toSet()) result.merge(frame, s.count, Long::plus) // once per sample } return result }

recap: A sampling profiler writes down thread stacks every few milliseconds and counts them. Collapsed stacks (a;b;c 42) are the common text format.

Profilers built on Thread.getStackTrace or JVMTI only see threads at safepoint polls, so samples land on the next poll: safepoint bias. Ours blamed String.split itself and never saw the methods it calls.
async-profiler interrupts threads with a signal and walks the stack where it landed, and it also sees native code, the JIT and GC threads and the kernel.
In a flame graph, width is samples, the root is at the bottom and left to right is alphabetical, not time. Wide bare tops are self time; follow them down to your own code.
Pick the mode for the question: cpu for CPU time, wall -t for waiting, alloc for who allocates, lock for contention. Use -e ctimer when perf_events is blocked.

The limit: a profile shows where time and bytes went during the seconds you recorded. It doesn't say which cost to remove first, or whether removing it helps the slow requests; that takes an investigation (lesson 7).

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate how to read the flame graph of a slow service: what width, height and left-to-right position mean, and how you get from the picture to the line of code to change.
explain.answer: Each box is a frame from the sampled stacks. Its width is how many samples had that frame there, so wide means a lot of time in it or in what it calls. Height is stack depth: callers below, callees above. Left to right means nothing, because frames at each level are sorted alphabetically, so it's not a timeline. I look for wide tops, the parts of boxes with nothing above them: that's where the CPU really was. Then I follow that tower down to the first frame in our own code, because I usually can't make a JDK method faster, but I can stop calling it so often. And if a profiler built on getStackTrace gives a surprising answer, I check it with async-profiler, because the simple ones only see threads at safepoints.

deeper.html:
Before version 4.2, async-profiler took Java stacks with AsyncGetCallTrace, a HotSpot function that isn't part of any standard API and that the profiler is named after. Its docs say it "was broken several times even in minor JDK updates" and could crash the JVM. That's why 4.2 made its own walker over HotSpot's internal structures the default (--cstack vm). vmx mode goes further and mixes Java and native frames in one stack.

-a (or --ann) marks frames by how they were compiled: _[j] for JIT-compiled methods, _[i] for inlined ones, _[0] for interpreted and _[1] for C1-compiled. That connects a profile back to lessons 1 and 2: a busy method stuck at _[0] or _[1] deserves a look with PrintCompilation.

Lesson 4 promised a symptom of false sharing: in a CPU profile, it shows up as a wide top on a line that does almost nothing, such as count++, because the thread spends its time waiting for the cache line.

Differential flame graphs compare two profiles. Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph tools colour frames "red for more, and blue for less", which is a quick way to see what a change did. Make both profiles the same length and under the same load, or the comparison measures the traffic instead of the code.

async-profiler can also write JFR files (-o jfr) that JDK Mission Control opens, and convert them later with jfrconv. With JMH, -prof async:libPath=<path to libasyncProfiler.so> runs it around a benchmark, so you get a flame graph of exactly the code you measured.
